*Researched outside this library — the knowledge base carries nothing on this passage. Sources are listed at the end.*

The letter of instruction was authored by **Maulana Ali ibn Abi Talib**, the fourth Caliph and the first Shia Imam. It is a renowned document included in the *Nahj al-Balagha* (The Peak of Eloquence), a collection of his sermons, letters, and sayings compiled by Sharif al-Radi.

The letter was addressed to his close and loyal companion, **Malik al-Ashtar**, a distinguished military commander. Maulana Ali appointed him to the office of **Governor of Egypt**, a vast and wealthy province at the time. This letter served as a comprehensive guide for just and righteous governance.

**Sources consulted**

- wikipedia.org

notes.body:
When this book speaks of 'the Nahj,' it means نَهْج الْبَلَاغَة, a title that can be rendered *the path of eloquence* — the single most treasured collection of the words of Maulana Ali. It gathers three kinds of speech into one volume: his sermons, his letters, and his short, piercing sayings. The long letter of counsel to Malik al-Ashtar, which this chapter unfolds, sits among its letters.

The man who assembled it was a scholar and poet known as al-Sharif al-Radi, working roughly three and a half centuries after Maulana Ali had passed. He was not writing history so much as preserving beauty and wisdom; **he chose the passages he found most eloquent and most morally luminous**, which is why the collection reads less like an archive and more like a distilled treasury.

Its standing is remarkable because it is honoured far beyond the community that reveres its author most deeply. Across the wider Muslim world it has long been placed just beneath two things:

- the Quran, the very speech of Allah,
- and the words of the Prophet Muhammad.

For Ismailis, and for Shia Muslims generally, the Nahj is more than fine literature; it is *guidance* from an Imam — a living map of how a soul should stand before Allah, and how a ruler should stand before those he governs. **That is why a single sentence from it can carry the weight of a whole teaching**: when the letter warns Malik against pride or against 'war with God,' it is not offering an opinion but drawing us back toward قِسْط, the balance at the heart of just rule.

Scholars have long debated whether every line can be traced word for word to Maulana Ali himself, and the honest ones admit some uncertainty. Yet even the most cautious agree on the essential point: the moral and spiritual vision breathing through these pages is unmistakably his, and it has shaped Muslim conscience for a thousand years.

etymology: نَهْج (path): from the root ن-ه-ج, a road that is wide, clear and openly trodden. A نَهْج is not a faint trail but a way so plain that no traveller can lose it — so the title itself promises a clear, unmistakable road leading straight into eloquence.

بَلَاغَة (eloquence): from the root ب-ل-غ, to reach or to arrive. Speech is called بَلِيغ when it *arrives* — carrying its full meaning all the way to the listener's mind and heart without anything lost along the road. Eloquence, then, is not ornament but words that reach their mark completely.

notes.body:
When the chapter calls Allah the **source** of a virtue, it means He is where that virtue comes from — the way water comes from a spring. The generosity we act with is not something we manufactured on our own; it flows down to us from Allah's own generosity, الکریم. He gives it, and we pass it on.

Calling Allah the **actual substance** of the virtue goes one step deeper. Grounded in تَوْحِيد, it says there is only one Reality, الحق, and every good quality that appears anywhere is truly His quality showing itself on a smaller scale. Our kindness is not a second, separate kindness standing beside Allah's — it is His kindness reflected in us.

The difference is easiest to feel through a **mirror**:

- as *source*, Allah is like the sun sending its light toward the glass;
- as *substance*, the brightness we see inside the glass is nothing but that same sunlight — not one particle of it belongs to the mirror.

So how can a divine quality be the very substance of what a created person does? Because we are the **mirror, never the sun**. The person is عبد, a servant who owns nothing of his own; the deed is genuinely his to perform, yet the light shining within it is borrowed. The Quran puts it exactly: 'And thou threw not when thou didst throw, but Allah it was who threw.'
Al-Anfal 8:17.

This is why the chapter ties everything back to **humility**. We stay generous for Allah's sake, because He is الرحمن الرحیم — never claiming to be generosity itself, only holding it up the way a mirror holds the sun.
notes.anchor: the actual substance of all human virtue
notes.quote: the actual substance of all human virtue
etymology: توحيد (declaring oneness): from the root و-ح-د, meaning to be one, single, alone. The form توحيد is the act of making or affirming oneness — actively holding that there is one Reality with no second. This is why it grounds the idea of 'substance': if only One truly is, every good quality is ultimately His.

عبد (servant): from the root ع-ب-د, to serve, worship, and obey. An عبد is one wholly given over to another's will, owning nothing of his own. Calling the human being عبد fixes his place exactly: he reflects Allah's qualities, he does not own them.

notes.body:
Think of standing before a mirror. The face looking back is truly ours, yet reversed — our right hand appears on the left. A reflection stays faithful to its original precisely by being flipped; un-inverted, it would not be a reflection at all but a second, rival face. That is the key: a divine quality does not repeat itself unchanged in us — **it appears in its human mode, which is its exact opposite.**

Allah's greatness is absolute; it belongs to Him alone. If our soul tried to catch that greatness faithfully — to hold it the way He holds it — we would be seizing His majesty for ourselves, and that is pride, the very rivalry the letter names as war with Allah. So the soul catches His transcendence the only honest way, **by inversion.** Where He is the Self-sufficient (الغني), we become the ones who own nothing and need Him for everything:

يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱللَّهُ هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ

O mankind, you are the destitute before Allah, and Allah is the Self-sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

Fatir 35:15

The mirror teaches the entire spiritual art in one image. To reflect His generosity we never announce 'I am generous'; we give for His sake alone, because He is the Generous (الکریم). Our share of the reflection is only **the emptied, servant-side of it** — the effacement, the lowliness — while the fullness stays wholly His.

So aiming at an inverted reflection means aiming at the right kind of resemblance. A true, un-flipped likeness would be idolatry; **an inverted likeness is worship.** The nearer we draw to Allah, the smaller we grow before Him — and that shrinking is not a failure but the exact shape His transcendence takes when it falls, truthfully, upon a human heart.
notes.anchor: what one sees is a reflection, but an inverted one
notes.quote: what one sees is a reflection, but an inverted one
etymology: الغني (the Self-sufficient): from the root غ-ن-ي, to be free of need, enriched and content in oneself. It names the One who requires nothing and from whom all enrichment flows — the very pole that our own neediness reflects, reversed.

الفقر (poverty): from the root ف-ق-ر, tied to فقار, the vertebrae of the spine. The فقیر is one whose backbone is bent by need, unable to stand alone — so the word names not empty pockets but the soul's utter dependence on Allah.

تَوْحِيد (making one): from the root و-ح-د, oneness. The form carries the sense of declaring and realising that oneness; the inverted reflection guards it, since it refuses to let any quality stand as a second alongside Allah's.
